utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to call its next witness? I'm asking you because although we had in mind to deal with some procedural matters, I'm not properly prepared at this moment and therefore the Chamber is not properly prepared. We'll do that as soon as possible, but I'd like to continue now not to discuss these procedural matters at this very moment but to do that at a later moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Your Honour, may we simply say that on behalf of the Defence team we do offer condolences for -- we understand Your Honour has suffered a personal loss and we offer our thoughts to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I received already in writing from both parties the -- their feelings, and I highly appreciate and -- and that's at the same time the explanation why we will not deal with the procedural matters at this moment. So therefore thank you very much. And you're ready --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The answer is yes, Your Honour, we are ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that will be a witness without any protective measures and it will be Mr. Micic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour, Mr. Momcilo Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Madam Usher, would you escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Micic. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honour. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before you give evidence in this court, Mr. Micic, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text will now be handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Micic. Please be seated. You'll be examined -- I take it by you, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, it's me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be examined by Mr. Stewart, who is counsel for the Defence. You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Micic. Mr. Micic, I'm going to run through a certain amount of what I believe will be basic background information, some of it personal to you and some relating to the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina back in 1990/1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, of course in the usual way, if anybody feels I'm crossing the line at any point, no doubt they will say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your name is Momcilo Micic. You were born on the 21st of January, 1939, in Bijeljina. You are a mechanical engineer by training and qualification. Up until 1990, you worked in a private firm, Ferotehnika in Tuzla. Is all that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you remained in Tuzla until the 14th of May, 1992, when you left for Belgrade, and your wife and your 25-year-old son, that's one of your two sons, on that day or the day before, also went to Belgrade. Is that right? We'll come back to these events in more detail, Mr. Micic, but what I've said so far is correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have lived in Belgrade ever since May 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a member of the communist party for 30 years until the collapse of communism in Yugoslavia and other places?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have never been a member of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No. No, I was never a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you join Ante Markovic's party, the SRS, when it was founded in the spring of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that you were active in launching that particular party in the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Tuzla region for these purposes consists, does it, of 19 municipalities - I've -- I hope I've eased the pain for the interpreters by given them a written list of these municipalities - but they are: Tuzla, Zevinice, Vukavak, Klodinje, Srebrenica, Zvornik, Sekovici, Bijeljina, Ugljevic, Lopari, Brcko, Gracanica, Vlasenica, Srebrenik, Orasje, Puracic, Banovce. Is that list correct? I missed one, did I?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You'll have to repeat your answer. It's you the interpreters didn't hear, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: And the municipality of Kalesija.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. What was your particular active role in relation to the SRS party in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I was the president of the party for the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there any sort of group or committee in which you were involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: We formed a party which had its statute, its bodies, its committees, subcommittees. It had everything that a political party was supposed to have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Tuzla, you lived in Tuzla at that time in 1990, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Tuzla had for -- I won't say always, but for a long time, for many, many years, if not decades, Tuzla had been the centre of the region constituted by the municipalities which I mentioned with your addition. That's right, is it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was pre-existing region which was adopted then after the collapse of communism?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Before that and afterwards. It was also a region during socialism, during the Socialist Federal Yugoslavia. And then later also it was a region in the multi-party system.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what do you remember as being the ethnic division of the town of Tuzla in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The town of Tuzla itself had about 130.000 inhabitants, 15 point something were Croats, 15 point something per cent were Serbs, 16 per cent I think were Yugoslavs, and I think about 43 per cents were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And approximately what was the population of the town of Tuzla at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: About 130.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time consider joining the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you summarise how you saw the differences between the SDS and the SRS in 1990 at the time -- well, in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The difference was in that we were a party of all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We were a party that was in favour of Yugoslavia. It did not differentiate in relation to the ethnic structure, while the SDS, the HDZ, and the SDA were purely national or nationalist parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it possible to say whether the SRS attracted a particular type of person from those different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how would you put that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: All those who thought a little differently than just purely from the national aspect. Bosnia is a republic that had a lot of basic industries and also was dependent on the economy of Serbia, Croatia, and was also reliant on those republics, especially Serbia, for its exports. So any kind of secession or any kind of inference in that would mean a loss of factories, a loss of markets, and would lead to a collapse. So all those who thought that you needed something to make a living from were actually those who supported us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you, as a representative of the SRS, attend SDS, SDA, and HDZ meetings in Tuzla in the course of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Only some meetings and purely out of courtesy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, first, in July 1990 did you attend an SDS inaugural meeting in a tennis stadium in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, in fact, there was a mining accident that very day which apparently significantly affected the attendance. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how many people did attend that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: A few scores of people, very few people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who from the -- if anybody, from the SDS leadership was present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand whether the witness said "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you repeat your answer, Mr. Micic. The interpreters could not hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were members of the SDS leadership present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who were present from the leadership?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I recall Radovan Karadzic being there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Local officials from Tuzla who were members of the SDS. I don't remember whether anyone else was there from Sarajevo or other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Krajisnik somebody who you would have recognised at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Naturally.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to say whether he was or might have been there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could Mrs. Plavsic have been there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Dr. Karadzic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any -- in the broader sense, was there any political content to your discussion with or -- with what passed between you and Dr. Karadzic on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No. I simply talked about the mining tragedy. There were about 80 miners killed in the mine, and I thought it was inappropriate to play music and to sing at the stadium in a town where there had been so many casualties. And I said that it would be good for them not to do that on that particular day, which he did not agree with. So after that, I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an SDA rally in some time around the middle of 1990 in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where any of the national leaders of the SDA present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which of them?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic was there and Silajdzic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There were local officials present, SDA leaders, and there were also members or the leaders of the MBO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you attended that rally, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say how many people were there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The meeting was held at the Tuzla hotel. There were a lot of people whom I didn't know, even though Tuzla is not a large town. More or less we all know each other, but there were a lot of people whom I didn't recognise. There were a lot of slogans. But there were a couple of hundred people, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the HDZ also hold a rally in or near Tuzla around the middle of 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it actually in Tuzla town?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It was in a neighbourhood near Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you attend that rally?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any difference that you saw in 1990 in the influence that those three parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, were able to achieve in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There was no difference between those three parties as far as their policies were concerned. They fought together against the former system, and they felt that that was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- did you stand for election to the Bosnia and Herzegovina parliament in the 1990 November elections, and were you elected?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before your involvement in the SRS in Tuzla, had you held any political positions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the -- in the municipality of Tuzla, what was the outcome in terms of voting in the 1990 -- November 1990 multi-party elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: In the town of Tuzla itself, the national parties won very few votes, practically nothing; the SRS and the League of Communists got the most votes. So we made a coalition of those two parties and formed the government in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall what were the relative votes achieved by your party and the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I believe it was -- I don't know, 39 or 43 -- no, we had 39 and the League of Communists had about 30. The SDA nine, I believe. The MBO probably seven. The HDZ around 5 per cent. And the SDS had 11 or 12 per cent or thereabouts. I can't be sure of the percentages, but that was more or less the situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally involved in power-sharing discussions in Tuzla following those elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, was it -- your party -- after the election, did your party remain a non-ethnic or multi-ethnic party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It was a multi-ethnic party. All the ethnic groups were represented.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there, within your party, any differences in the approach of -- within the membership of your own party I'm asking, were there any differences in the approach of the different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Initially not. However, when the municipal government was established, then the differences could be felt.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what were those differences that could be felt?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Since we established a coalition with the SDP, which was the former League of Communists, and we formed power together, we had joined meetings in order to distribute positions in the local government. Nobody else could be given any position but the Muslims, and both parties had members of the Muslim ethnic group who supported those proposals for Muslim holders of various positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then what was your personal attitude towards that position adopted by the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At that moment there were no major objections, because the people appointed were professionals and had skills and knowledge for the positions that they were appointed to. We didn't care much about the ethnicity of those people; we just wanted them to be up to the positions to which they were being appointed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, who was Mehmed Bajric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Mehmed Bajric was the chief of the municipal secretariat of the interior. He was in that position even before. He was the chief of the secretariat of the municipality of Tuzla, and he was a non-party candidate; he did not belong to any party. I believe that he should stay in that position because he had proven himself as a professional.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct he was -- are you saying he was not even formally a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that. Formally he was a member of the League of Communists, and once the police was depoliticised, or at least that's how they wished to be perceived, I did not object to him remaining in that position because he was a professional. He knew the job well at that moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was a Muslim, was he, Mehmed Bajric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the chief of the regional interior was Budimir Nikolic, who was a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally adopting any public position in relation to the future of the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At the moment of the elections, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you subsequently -- well, either before or after, did you at any time adopt a public position in relation specifically to the future of the Tuzla region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, well, first of all, when was that? Before or after the elections?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: After the elections.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was that position that you adopted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: My position was for a civic Tuzla. Tuzla is an industrial complex that was a very powerful complex with basic industry, and its produce was mostly sold in Serbia. And once polarisation took place, I used the local television and the local press to bring people to their senses. There was even an initiative initially, and it was supported by all, for Tuzla to be separated from the rest of Bosnia and to remain in Yugoslavia. However, that initiative fell through very quickly because all who were in power at the moment were mostly of Muslim ethnicity. And little by little they all opted for the SDA policies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That initiative that you describe as having fell through, was that one that you personally supported?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It implied, did it, that Bosnia and Herzegovina would otherwise become independent from the rest of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Well, if it could not remain in Yugoslavia, at least for it to become independent or remain independent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Turning to the National Assembly, the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly, after the election, it's correct, is it, that at the first session Mr. Krajisnik was unanimously elected as the president of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unanimously on behalf of the three national parties. We did not vote for that proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it's the position that -- so the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ deputies, did they unanimously support Mr. Krajisnik's election as president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the members of your party adopt a group position and all vote the same way on that issue?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At that moment, yes. We were opposed to any election using the national quota, not only of the president of the Assembly, his deputy, and the secretary, but also prime minister, members of parliament, everybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you abstain or vote against the proposals?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I believe that we were against.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that Mr. Mariofil Ljubic of the HDZ was elected vice-president and Mr. Avdo Campara of the SDA was elected secretary of the parliament?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer and speak perhaps a bit more close to the microphone so that the interpreters can better hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Momcilo Krajisnik was elected president; Mariofil Ljubic was elected vice-president, and Sead Avdic was elected the secretary of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct that the Assembly assisted of two Chambers, the citizens' council to which you belonged, chaired by Mustafa Konjicija of the SDA, and the Council of Municipalities chaired by Petko Cancar of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to the constitution of the municipality, it was a two-chamber assembly with a house of citizens and a house of municipality and a council for national equality. In other words, it had three separate council or houses, which was provided for by the constitution.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was to be the -- as you understood it at the time, what was to be the position of the -- role of the Council for National Equality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina consists of three constituent ethnic groups: Muslims, Serbs, and Croats. And in order to avoid outvoting on certain issues on the agenda or any other issue, the constitution provided for 20 MPs to be able to take that off the agenda and for this to be referred to the Council for National Equality where it would be a consensus who would decide on that. Until this moment, this council never took off the ground. It was never even established because the Muslim and Croat representatives refused to do that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was -- well, was your attitude - and we'll come to what it was in a moment - but was your attitude towards that refusal by the Muslim and Croat representatives the same as that of your own party colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: We were the first ones to request that, and we even drafted a request to that effect. We wanted the council to be established. But the president of the council at the time, Mustafa Konjic, turned the proposal down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your party had 13 members -- deputies in the parliament at that time. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many of those were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the -- was the proposal to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You said that the Council for National Equality never took off the ground, was never even established. Was there any step taken by any leading member of the SDS to try to get that body established and off the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember when any such steps were first taken by leading members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was the one who made several attempts to put this on the agenda of the Assembly, for the council to be established; this was in the second half of 1991. But this was never adopted as an item on the agenda because the Muslims and the Croats were always against that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was your own attitude towards Mr. Krajisnik's proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: We supported that proposal. I personally supported it because I thought that this was the only thing that would provide for the equality of all the three peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your personal -- was your support -- was support also given by your colleagues in the SRS among the deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All of them or was there some division of view among the SRS deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Not at the time. We were all in favour of this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there at some point emerge any significant difference of views among the SRS deputies in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that first occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: This happened when the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina held some of their meetings in the absence of other members. Only the Muslims and the Croats attended those meetings and made decisions that were supposed to be implemented and when the coalition between the SDA and the HDZ was already very clear. They sent a request to the JNA to leave Bosnia because they were a hostile army. That is when a polarisation took place in the SRS itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any of your colleagues among the SRS deputies participate in those meetings and in those decisions referred to in your last answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The four of us who were Serbs in the SRS were also members of the Main Board of the SRS for Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this is what was taking place at the Main Board of the SRS of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you to clarify. When you say: "This is what was taking place at the Main Board of the SRS," could you be rather more specific as to what it was that was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The Main Board of the SRS considered the newly arisen political situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina and opted for some positions and gave directives to the MPs as to how they were supposed to behave in the Republican Assembly. We were -- we had some disagreements about the army. Some were in favour of the army staying, for it to be a multi-national rather than mono-national. Alija didn't want Muslims to go to the army, that they should leave the army. Truth be told, only the foot-soldiers were being referred to; the officers remained in the army. And this is where we divided, whether the JNA should be a multi-national or for the two nations to leave the JNA. This is what we could not agree on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How would you describe relations among the three national parties, the SDA, the SDS, and the HDZ, in the first two or three months after the multi-party elections in November 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I'll try to answer your question. The relationship, if you are asking me about the relationship between the three multi-national -- mono-national parties, at the beginning those relationship [as interpreted] was very good. We had common positions, if that was your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there at any point any significant change?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Those changes took place when there was a -- over voting when there was an informal coalition between the SDA and the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to put a question to the witness, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm very sorry, Mr. Stewart, for this. Before you go any further, I would like to seek some clarification on two points from the witness and this is to do with the Assembly. He told us that there was the citizens' chamber and the chamber for the municipalities. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you be more specific. How were they made up, respectively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the election results, those houses consisted of Croats, Serbs, and Muslims. I wouldn't be able to give you the exact percentages of those three peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In what were they different?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The house of citizens was elected from the electoral units which were below the region. For example, the municipality of Tuzla gave five or six MPs into the -- into the Assembly. And all the other municipalities were entitled to one MP in the house of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for a bill to be passed, did it have to be submitted to both houses? If there was a vote on a bill, did it have to go through the two houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some yes, some no. Those that concerned the municipal government, the local government, it sufficed for the house of municipalities to vote on those. As for the bills that concerned the entire republic, it was the house of citizens that did that. There were also bills that had to be voted on by both houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is about the Council of National Equality. I didn't quite get what its role was. Could you describe it again for me. What should its role have been? What was the role it had under the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the constitution, this council had to have an equal number of members from all the three constituent peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And whatever 20 MPs believed could be harmful and at the expense of one ethnic group, they could ask for such an item to be taken off the agenda and referred to the council. The council was then supposed to consider such an item among themselves, and they were supposed to come up with a joint position on such an item in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did the Muslims and the Croats not want to see this body work? What kind of explanation do you have for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my private opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Croats were in favour of the secession of Bosnia because the secession of Croatia had already been underway. And Muslims believed that that's -- that was the way for them to get their own republic with the help of the Croats, because both groups were in favour of the civic Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and they were not in favour of the civic state of Yugoslavia, which was much better in respecting human and civic rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. If we keep in mind the first, the inaugural session in Tuzla in July 1990, you said that you had an opportunity to speak to Radovan Karadzic. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, we know - and this is not in dispute, the Trial Chamber has heard a lot of evidence already about it - there was a crisis in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly in the middle of October 1991; that's well-established. Was there any sort of crisis or anything approaching a crisis before that date?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There were attempts in the form of various questions about the future of Bosnia, the secession of Bosnia, and so on. So there were heated debates between the parties, but in the end, thanks to a rational policy conducted by Mr. Krajisnik, everything would calm down and some sort of order would be brought back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was Mr. Krajisnik -- was Mr. Krajisnik, for practical purposes, always present at Assembly sessions as president?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his own participation when such heated debates occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is a pragmatic person. He tried to calm down the situation and to find a solution which would be good for both sides.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any member of the Bosnian -- of the SDS leadership, I beg your pardon, did any member of the SDS leadership at any time before October 1991 bring any sort of pressure on you or your colleagues in the SRS in relation to voting in parliament?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- I'll -- again, I'll take the period up to October 1991. Did you ever meet Mr. Krajisnik in any way in connection with parliamentary business?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say for the period from the elections in November 1990 up to the crisis which I mentioned in October 1991 how often or how many times you met Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: A couple of times, two or three times. I think the first time I met Mr. Krajisnik was when -- when I left the SRS because of the earlier described events, and then there was a request that we were going to lose our mandate. This was done by the party, because we had left the party. But since the party was dead anyway -- I mean, we stayed in the Assembly. So that was the first question because of which I went to see Mr. Krajisnik, not in order to attempt to persuade him to stay, but just to hear what his views were on the topic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just first, then, in the light of that answer, Mr. Micic, ask you when was it that you left the SRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It's difficult to give the exact date, but once we left the SRS we made a statement for the then-daily Oslobodjenja, so this is something that you can then establish what date it was exactly because Oslobodjenja published this information. In any case, it was perhaps two or three months before the crisis that then happened in the Assembly, perhaps even more than that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- well, how many of the SRS deputies left the party at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were those the four Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there something specific which triggered off or finally provoked you to leave the party?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I already explained at the beginning that there was a misunderstanding relating to the implementation of the mobilisation to the ranks of the Yugoslav People's Army and the demand that the Yugoslav People's Army be ruled out, because that was when the Muslims had already began to create the Patriotic League as well as some kind of reserve police forces. We believed that two armies in one terrain or territory could only fight, and we did not support this because we felt it was leading to war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, first of all, can we be clear, you say there was a misunderstanding relating to the implementation of mobilisation. Between whom was that misunderstanding?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Alija first publicly addressed the nation asking that recruits, Muslims, do not go to the army; and for those who were already in the army, to leave it. So it was a public call. And then there were problems caused by this between the army and the local branches that were carrying out the recruitment, because the recruitment because carried out by centres in the municipalities and not by the army. So then there were problems and disagreements in relation to this. We were outvoted on this without any proper documents or any proper explanation that this would be a wise move. It was just simply a decision not to join the army and to form two armies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What specifically were you outvoted on?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: On the question of the recruitment of conscripts and regarding the documentation which was being kept in the recruitment centres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this was a motion or proposal put forward in the Assembly, was it, on which you were outvoted?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I am talking about the Main Board of the party; this is still not about the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Mr. Micic. Who -- within the Main Board of your party, who put forward this proposal?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think that it was Dzevad Sokolovic, Professor Dzevad Sokolovic, who was actually not a deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you -- did you formally resign, then, from the SRS?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did that have any effect upon your status as a deputy in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anybody else suggest that it did have any effect upon your status as a deputy in that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: SRS officially demanded from the Assembly to strip us of our mandates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, were they successful?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How were they blocked from stripping you of your mandate?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think that the request was sent as a formal course of action. Nobody actually asked for this to be put on the agenda, so this is not something that was actually discussed by the Assembly itself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know why it did not get on the agenda?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No, I don't. I said that no official deputy asked for it to be placed on the agenda, or at least I don't know if such a request was made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- were you present on the night of the 14th and 15th of October, 1991, in the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly when the Serb deputies at some point walked out?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how would you describe Mr. Krajisnik's handling of that situation?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: He behaved the way he behaved up until that time. He tried, in a way, to bring some sense to this matter, to kind of deal with this problem in a different way, to put it off, to perhaps send it to the constitutional commission. But the position of the SDA and the HDZ was quite firm, and nothing could be done about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- you continued, did you, after that crisis as a member of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you at that time had any meeting with Dr. Karadzic since the time that you had met him in Tuzla way back in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At the Assembly, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about outside the Assembly? And I'm talking about the period now between when you met him at that rally in Tuzla in 1990 and mid-October 1991 when there was the parliamentary crisis. Did you --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No, not since October, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, you say "not since October," just so that we --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Until October, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you after mid-October and that parliamentary crisis meet Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was -- whether or not it was more than one occasion, when did you first meet Dr. Karadzic after mid-October 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think in early 1992, perhaps sometime in March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And upon whose initiative did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: On my initiative.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anybody else at that meeting, apart from you and Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who else was present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was there as well as the general of the Tuzla Corps command, General Jankovic, as well as his security chief, Milomir. I really don't remember what his surname is at the moment. He was a colonel. Rasulovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there anybody else who was a member of the SDS present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think Professor Aleksa Buha was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the reason -- if there was one, what was the reason for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The reason for the meeting was simply for me as well as General Jankovic, who was at the time the corps commander of the Tuzla corps, to hear what the SDS thought about the coming period so that we could form our own position. We wanted to get some information.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who in that context is we? You said: "We wanted to get some information."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: At the time the Tuzla municipality was still a civic one and it was very homogenous in its actions. So we tried to get some information from all three of the national parties. We tried to see what their positions were, what they were thinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was General Jankovic there with you, as it were, with you going with him to find out jointly these matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did General Jankovic participate with you in that way?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I knew General Jankovic personally. I was on not friendly terms with him, but we were acquaintances. And it was question for him as a corps commander what to do, how to do things regarding the question of whether the army would remain there or not. We just needed to know what the positions were. We needed to get this directly rather than just hear about it from the radio or television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you travel from Tuzla with General Jankovic to Sarajevo for that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did others of your colleagues from Tuzla travel to Sarajevo at the same time for a meeting or meetings there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you and General Jankovic hold any other meetings or attend any other meetings on that visit to Sarajevo, apart from the one with Dr. Karadzic and the people you've mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you on any other occasions hold meetings with any other representatives of any other political party in Sarajevo in connection with the concerns you've indicated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before or after the meeting with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long before?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think in late 1990 -- no, 1991, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And with what other political party or parties did you hold any such meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I was in the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was with Minister Delimustafic. He was the minister for internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your position in the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I didn't have a position. I was not a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said you were in the government. In what sense then were you in the government?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I was with the president of the Tuzla Executive Council together at that meeting at Delimustafic's with the intention of trying to keep these two people at the regional SUP and also at the municipal secretariat for internal affairs, which by the party distribution of those posts were given to others and they were supposed to be replaced, Dr. Sead Avdic and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The two people you've just referred to in your answer, you said: "With the intention of trying to keep these two people at the regional but also the municipal secretariat," who were the two people?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I was thinking of Mehmed Bajric and Budimir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go back then, please, to the meeting that you held with -- you described with Dr. Karadzic and others you mentioned. Was Professor Koljevic present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It's possible. I can't be certain, but I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've already told Their Honours that it was at your instigation or initiative that the meeting was set up. Did you at the meeting put any proposals, questions, or items for discussion to Dr. Karadzic or his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what then?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: We talked about the position of the Yugoslav People's Army in the territory that was covered by that corps, and we wanted to see whether the SDS, at the time one of the ruling parties, whether they had any thoughts on that, any plans. We wanted to get some information. So it was the eastern corps, the corps in the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you get information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an expressed or apparent refusal to give you information?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what was your assessment of why you did not get the information you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: First of all, we wanted to hear the programme, what the objectives were. Then we understood that there was no programme and there were no objectives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're talking about the objectives of the SDS, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there -- well, before you started the meeting, did you have an opinion as to what the essential objectives of the SDS were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I personally think that the SDS is a forced party. It's a popular movement created as a reaction to the forming of the Muslim party, the SDA, and the HDZ, too. And I think the HDZ was actually formed later, but I think that it was an organisation, a peoples', citizens' movement that didn't have any clear objectives, positions, or any direction in what it wanted, other than to be a partner in relation to these other two parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Micic, I don't believe there's going to be any challenge or dispute about this. One thing was clear, wasn't it, that the SDS wished to preserve Bosnia and Herzegovina as part of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was also the objective of my party because we were the alliance of reform forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to request that counsel be a bit more cautious about leading. I think that's something that's been made clear in the Prosecution's case. It's a bit of a time-sensitive issue. Positions and policies change over the time, so I would prefer to find out from the witness what he understands about SDS positions, rather than being told what an SDS position might or might not be at a particular point in time and simply assenting. I'm not suggesting any attempt, any inappropriate motive on counsel's part, but I would just like to urge that approach from this point forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't mind, Your Honour, if I'm going to be that cautious, then Mr. Tieger might have to clear his diary for some considerable time to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Stewart, of course there is an issue when the witness testified that there were no clear objectives, and we are talking -- I don't know exactly what time. And then you said -- you put a question to him to see that there's hardly dispute about -- of course there could be a dispute about whether the SDS had any objectives, yes or no. I mean, that's what the witness testified, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm in Your Honour's hands. I will be as cautious -- I said I will be as cautious as I'm required to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where the witness testifies that there were no clear objectives of the SDS, perhaps we could have heard from the witness whether he was talking about a certain period of time. Because this question follows a long line of questioning on meetings in early 1992, and therefore I think -- I would agree with Mr. Tieger that without inviting you to spend days and days on it, to be especially at this point -- there were good reasons for being cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will be then. Now I see how cautious I need to be, and I shall be that cautious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time that you had this meeting with Dr. Karadzic, before the meeting, before the meeting started, did you have any idea of any essential strands of SDS party policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what idea did you have?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I said that at the very beginning. The HDZ and the SDA had a certain interest in the secession of Bosnia, not only of Croatia, and that would have made the job of Croatians easier. The Serbs were not interested in the separation of the Serb people along the Drina River. There were various reasons, not only emotional, religious, and ethnic ones. The priority reasons were economic reasons, and for that reason there was a plebiscite for Serbs to opt for saying in Yugoslavia. The SDS thought that Yugoslavia should be preserved in any -- within any borders and that Bosnia should be kept within that Yugoslavia. Because the question was: Why should it have not been kept in Yugoslavia since it was already a civic republic of a civic state. That was my information. When I said there were no goals, there were no objectives, I meant the specific conversation that took place at the Holiday Inn hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now you've told Their Honours that as far as you recall this meeting was in early 1992 and you mentioned March. At the time of this meeting, did you have some -- were you in a position to make some personal assessment of how far momentum had been gathered towards independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was already a beginning of chaos. Some people just couldn't cope. That's how I understood Radovan. Radovan simply did not have a clear picture as to what he should have done at the moment, what he was supposed to do at the moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see the SDA at that particular point as having a clear policy? The SDA I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you see as their policy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Their policy was to create an Islamic republic in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the help of the HDZ. They expected that they would get that support and that they would be able to realise their goal. The basis for that was the Islamic declaration written by Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said a couple of answers ago that "Radovan simply did not have a clear picture as to what he should have done at the moment, what he was supposed to do at the moment." Did he - from what you could tell - have a clear picture about anything?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The information that could be obtained at the time from various corners of the republic about reactions, names, proclamations, I don't think he had a clear picture. What I'm saying is that there was no project telling us what to do. I may be speaking as an engineer here, but I think that in every job there should be a project, that there should be a design that guides people when they have a job to do. And this is what we were after, a project, a design.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- did what you heard from Dr. Karadzic or his colleagues at that meeting match your expectations of the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I expected more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What more had you expected?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I thought that every serious party - and the SDS perceived itself as a serious party - should have a programme, a policy. At the moment when we were there, we should have been told how to do things, how to remedy some things that were wrong.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- was this short-fall, as against your expectations, something that you communicated to Dr. Karadzic at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What -- what was Mr. Krajisnik's participation in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: He kept quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm just looking at the clock. I think it's just an hour and a half since we began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we had a bit of a late start. I'm just wondering whether we could have one break, a bit longer, rather than two breaks. If we would continue until quarter to 5.00, then have a break of 35 minutes; and then to continue until 7.00, would that be agreeable for the interpreters and technicians? So have a bit of a longer break, because if we take two breaks, they both have to be at least 20 minutes. And this is perhaps a way of dealing with it. Is there any objection from those who are assisting us? I do not hear, but I should perhaps also listen to the French and the B/C/S booth.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please continue, Mr. Stewart, for another seven minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we welcome that course. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, was any -- specifically any expressed at that meeting by Dr. Karadzic or any colleague of his as to their attitude towards the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Their attitude towards the JNA was correct and the JNA was supported. They believed that the JNA should stay in the area because the JNA was a guarantee of peace, a guarantee that nothing would happen, a guarantee for the people. There was a fear that once the JNA withdrew, that there would be an exodus of the Serbian people. This was discussed, but we couldn't hear any concrete agreement as to how and when to organise that. The JNA could not count on any support by the SDS for doing that. All that they could receive from the SDS were their good wishes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you -- did you form any impression at that meeting as to whether on any level there was any sort of agreement between the SDS leadership and senior officers in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No. As far as I know, the JNA officers did not respect any national party. They did that to the extent they had to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have, before or after that meeting, private discussion with General Jankovic about what you thought might happen at the meeting or, if it was afterwards, what had happened at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: We arrived in the same car, and we did talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you talked after the meeting as well, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any -- from your discussion with General Jankovic after the meeting, was there any difference of impression or view between you and him about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There was a feeling of disappointment with the situation. I believe that General Jankovic had expected to hear some talks about the support of the international community or that sort of discussion, but this did not happen. And I believe that soon after that he took some measures in order to move the corps out of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask one clarification with the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of your answers, one of yours previous answers, Mr. Micic started where you said -- it just went off my screen. "Their attitude," and that was the attitude of your interlocutors at that meeting, Mr. Karadzic, "their attitude towards the JNA was correct and the JNA was supported. They believed that the JNA should stay in the area because the JNA was a guarantee of peace, a guarantee that nothing would happen, a guarantee for the people." And then a few lines later you said: "We couldn't hear any concrete agreement as to how and when to organise that." I don't understand that to be, but please correct me when I understood you wrong, to organise that the JNA would stay where they were in order to avoid an exodus of the Serbian people. And then you continue to say: "The JNA could not count on any support by the SDS for doing that. All that they could receive from the SDS were their good wishes." Now, the beginning of your answer very much suggests that the people you were talking with were very much in support of the JNA staying there, being a guarantee for peace. And at the end of your answer you say: "They could -- the JNA could not count on any support." How do I have to understand these two portions of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as your question is concerned, the JNA was a -- an army of mixed composition consisting of the three peoples. As I already said, Alija wanted the foot-soldiers to leave the JNA; the officers remained. All the colonels of Muslim and Croat ethnic remained in the Tuzla corps. We believed that a multi-ethnic army is the only one that could guarantee peace. A mono-ethnic army or any newly formed army could not have done that. And as to your question why only good wishes, for an army requires logistics not just verbal support by somebody in the Assembly, if I have understood your question well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, not really. Of course, I did not expect the Assembly to provide for the logistics. But in the beginning of your answer it sounds as if the -- Mr. Karadzic was in favour of the JNA staying, and the second part of your answer you said the JNA could not count on any support by the SDS for doing that, which, as I understand, was - but please correct me when my understanding is wrong - to avoid that by withdrawing they would cause an exodus of the Serbian people. So the beginning of your answer seems to express support by Dr. Karadzic; the second part of your answer - and that's confirmed in one of your later answers - seems that the JNA could not count on the support. I have some difficulties to combine these two answers -- two parts of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS policy was to absolutely support Yugoslavia, and with that to the Yugoslav People's Army. When Alija published his declaration, when the Patriotic League was formed, there was an objective danger that there would be a conflict between these two militaries. We thought that we should receive a programme, a position, that would be our guideline as to where, how, and on what places we could count on because this corps covered the entire north-eastern Bosnia. We were not satisfied only with a programme. We wanted to know exactly what municipalities should be the future locations where the JNA could withdraw. Those were our thoughts, but we did not get any thoughts in return from Dr. Karadzic. And this is the support that was missing, that was not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I do understand that where you got a kind of a general political support, that Dr. Karadzic failed to give - from what I understand - you expected, to give more concrete support to say, well, this is to be done; that's where we go, you have to go; and to find a kind of -- well, to say a kind of plan on the role of the JNA in those areas rather than general political support. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What did you expect Dr. Karadzic could have done? I mean, your expectations were not just general political support. Did you think that Dr. Karadzic had the means to give the logistical, tactical guidance you were seeking?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We knew he didn’t because he didn’t have any role in the government. He was the president of the party. He wasn’t even a member of the Presidency; I don’t think he had any power. We simply tried to obtain some information, any sort of information, so as to be able to draw up our own plans and programmes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How could you be disappointed if you said he was just a member of parliament and was really not even a member of Presidency? You addressed him. You didn't got what you were seeking; you were disappointed. How could you be disappointed if he had not been in a position where he could have given you what you expected? I mean, I'm trying to understand your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, we do believe, and Mr. Sladojevic confesses that there is some sort of mistranslation on the transcript and the answer that begins "we knew he did not have any such thing." It seemed to me, actually, just on the sense of it there might be. Mr. Sladojevic, with the linguistic advantage, says that he believes there was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please sort that out then during the next break to see what problem there is and inform the Chamber in such a way that it doesn't give any clue to the witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- on what the issue is. But before doing so, I've got one other question. You told us that you were seeking to get information from three parties and that you met with the other two, I understand SDA and HDZ, before you went to see Mr. Karadzic. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not me who went. It had been agreed by the bodies of Tuzla, the president of the municipality, Selim Beslagic, was to try to talk to the MBO and the SDA. And after that we were supposed to obtain some common information. We were the opposition, and information was not given readily to us. And that's why we tried to obtain that information, and that's how we operated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say -- but let me just try to be sure that I fully understood you. You say: "It wasn't me who went," so that means that you didn't go to the SDA, you didn't -- you did not attend a meeting with the SDA or a meeting with the HDZ to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So where the question was, page 27, line 25: "Did you at any other occasion hold meetings with any other representatives of any other political parties in Sarajevo in connection with the concerns you have indicated?" You answered: "Yes." And then you said: "Before or after the meeting with Dr. Karadzic? "Before." Do I have to understand this that you didn't have meetings with the other parties but, well, let's say, other people from Tuzla more affiliated with SDA would have meetings with the SDA, and others more affiliated with the HDZ would meet with the HDZ people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not understand the question in that way. I didn't understand that you were focussed on that meeting with three ethnic parties. The way I understood it was whether at any time I was at a meeting with these parties, and I said yes. I was in the government building when I tried to keep the chiefs of the SUP. Those two things have nothing to do with each other. The Defence counsel did not ask me why I went to those meeting [as interpreted]; he only asked me if I went, and I said that I did go to these meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You earlier -- talking about these meetings, you said: "We tried to see what their positions were," and you were talking about the national parties, "what they were thinking." Later on you testified about your meeting with Dr. Karadzic and you said that meetings with the two other parties were held before that. Now, did you participate in these two other meetings with, I take it, the two other parties being SDA and HDZ, before you had a meeting with Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not. Have you information about these meetings? Who went to these other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Meetings with the SDA and the MBO, it was to be the then-president of the municipality, Selim Beslagic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, was General Jankovic also present during those meetings which you did not attend with the other parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, I did understand that you in Tuzla were trying to find out the positions of the other parties. The two others go there -- well, perhaps not alone, but were they accompanied by any JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so -- actually, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Why was the meeting with the SDS not [sic] a meeting with a Tuzla Serbian official together with a JNA officer, whereas the other two went to their national parties without someone from the JNA being present?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, is there a wrong "not" in that answer, Your Honour, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read again. The "not" is wrong, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I had in mind, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. So my question -- and it was -- I must have made a mistake. Why -- let's keep it simple. Why did the others go to their national parties without a JNA officer? And why did you go to the SDS with a JNA officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS supported the Yugoslav variant of Bosnia and Herzegovina and it supported the JNA, whereas the HDZ and the SDA were opposed to both. So it would have been pointless to have a JNA officer attending a meeting where he would not have been welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we still have enough tape for one more question? If not, I'd like to hear from you. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you just said that the JNA was a -- was to be multi-ethnic in order to maintain the safety of the inhabitants. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So were you expecting that Mr. Karadzic shares that point of view? Did you expect him to say that he was also absolutely convinced that the JNA should be multi-ethnical [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was no dispute about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he contest it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He advocated that, a multi-party army, an army of all citizens, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll now have a break until 5.35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I'd like to make one observation in relation to scheduling this week. The Chamber is considering to sit on Thursday, both morning and afternoon, and then we have of course a bit shorter sessions because we can't have ten hours. We then hope that we'll finish with both witnesses of this week by Thursday. If not, then Rule 15 bis might apply. That means that since I will not be available for urgent personal reasons next Friday, the two other Judges will then decide whether to sit, the two of them, it will only be one day, and not more, and I think it's limited to five days. So that's what the Chamber is considering. If, especially, the Thursday would cause great problems, then of course the Chamber would like to know before taking a final decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just say on that point, Your Honour, we -- if we may, we'd like to take it under advisement, as they say, and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're not inclined to be obstructive, Your Honour, but we would like the opportunity of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand, of course. But then at least you know what the Chamber has on its mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And of a course a decision would be taken relatively soon. Then please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. So far as that translation point was concerned, it turned out to be procedurally a little bit more difficult to sort out than one perhaps expected. But I understand that if I issue an invitation, I think, to the interpreter's booth to help us on that, it was at page 39, line 3, was where the answer began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there any page 33 -- it might be difficult for the interpreters to verify or to consider whether, as usually is case, gave the perfect translation, but of course now and then it's a human job. But then of course it might be difficult for them to do that if they have not heard the original again. So therefore, I would say if the interpreters -- you said page 33, line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 39, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, perhaps I made the mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 39, line 3 was where the relevant answer started and the particular point was on the next line then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It now reads at this moment: "We knew he did not have any such thing. He was not anything in the party; he was just a member of parliament." That's the lines you're referring to, Mr. Stewart?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I think Your Honour can see how applied to that particular person, at least a question arises.
