utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the interpreters could safely on their recollection, on their recollection of what was said in the original, tell us whether there could be any doubt on the correctness of the interpretation, they're invited to do so. Otherwise, we'll see that the original portion of the audiotape is reproduced in such a way that the interpreters can, with that in their mind, give the answers to the questions put to them. May I hear from the interpretation -- from the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There may have been a misunderstanding, but the interpreter cannot remember the exact words that the witness used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we'll have to find the original audiotape and see whether there's any mistake. We will sit tomorrow in the afternoon. I'm quite confident that it could be done tomorrow in the morning. We have now clearly identified which portion it is, so therefore I think we can clarify the matter tomorrow in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly not urgent now for today, Your Honour. That's entirely satisfactory. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, was there -- was there any expression of expectation by Dr. Karadzic or his colleagues at that meeting in 1992 as to what the army might be imminently going to do?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any -- first of all, let me ask you this: The -- can you say with confidence whether this meeting with Dr. Karadzic that you've described was before or after the European Union recognition of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It was after the Serb deputies left the Assembly, the joint Assembly, in any case and on the declaration of the memorandum on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina by the Muslim and Croat delegates of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I couldn't really say whether it was before or after recognition. I think that it was before recognition, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- was there any discussion at that meeting with Dr. Karadzic about ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No. There was no discussion about the ethnic division of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any discussion about any imminent risk of violence and conflict?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the nature of that discussion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The arming of a part of the Muslim population by the Muslim Patriotic League and the police reserve was discussed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you say who raised that topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The topic was raised by General Jankovic. He had information, probably through his intelligence service.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what information did he have?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say. But he did assert that certain groups of people were arming themselves and that preparations were being made.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any reaction from Dr. Karadzic and his colleagues to what General Jankovic said on that topic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think that they knew about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, by the time you had this meeting with Dr. Karadzic, had you personally become a member of the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And had you already attended at least one meeting, a session, of that Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any significant differences of view within the SDS as to the developing difficulties between the SDS on the one hand and the SDA/HDZ on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll slightly rephrase it, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you include the source of knowledge from what happened within the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I -- it may be covered by my rephrasing of this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what you were able to observe within the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Mr. Micic, did it appear that there were any significant differences of view among the SDS deputies in that Assembly as to the developing difficulties between the SDS on the one hand and the SDA and HDZ on the other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- who appeared, if anybody, to lead the views and policies of the SDS deputies and the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You -- there was nobody who clearly led those views and policies. Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's -- when a question is asked that doesn't call for a yes or no question [sic], it may have simply been misunderstood. I don't think it's an invitation to a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well I accept that, Your Honour. I'm trying to steer the line to get the clarification. If you'll allow me just to see how I might best meet Mr. Tieger's concerns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you could meet his concerns, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to do; it would certainly be appreciated by him, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- who were -- were there among the Bosnian Serb -- the SDS deputies in the Bosnian Serb Assembly, were there some who were more vociferous than others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Well, in every Assembly you have people who talk a lot, those who don't talk so much or little, but I don't think that those who are more vociferous have more influence or affect the work of the Assembly more just by that very fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there then among the deputies any that you can identify as having more influence, effect, or impact in the Assembly sessions?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. People were different in terms of who could be expected to express their position more eloquently or less eloquently. But I don't really know if anybody was consistently like that. Perhaps if once they were very eloquent in explaining their point, it wouldn't mean that they would always be as eloquent whenever they spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there in the Bosnian Serb Assembly SDS members that you can identify with whom you, for practical purposes, agreed on the important issues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There were, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you, therefore, identify who those members were?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Mostly we had a similar position. There were about nine of us independent deputies, from the SRS, from the League of Communists, from the Socialist Alliance, and I don't know what other party it was. But there were a total of nine of us, and we had the same opinions and we represented the opposition in that Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in representing the opposition, were there -- and I'm focussing on the time of the meeting you described, so I'm focussing on March 1992. Were there issues and points in which you, the opposition, took a different view from the prevailing view in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: If you're thinking about the visit, I didn't talk about the visit at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, just to clarify, I wasn't asking about the visit; I was asking about the Bosnian Serb Assembly sessions. You've told Their Honours you and your eight colleagues were the opposition, and I'm asking you whether from that opposition position you took a different view on any issues from the prevailing view in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not always, but yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify any points of, in your view, significance on which you took a different view?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about different laws that were being adopted concerning the economy and the various taxes imposed by the state on the economy, we viewed that differently and explained it differently. And we always sought to have a more realistic basis for such things, according to our views.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you personally support the Cutileiro Plan and the Lisbon and Sarajevo agreements?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your eight colleagues in opposition also support those matters?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have -- and I'm talking about you individually. Did you have at that time, in March 1992, any significant difference of view from Dr. Karadzic on any of the current political issues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The only thing I wanted was to avoid any kind of conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have proposals to make on how that could be done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It was difficult to suggest anything sensible or clever at that time. It was simply an attempt to seek some kind of understanding, some kind of backing away or compromise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As conflict emerged - and I'm talking about armed conflict in April 1992 - did any differences of view emerge among the SDS deputies in the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you identify such differences and between whom they arose?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There were differences in the way the situation was understood and assessed. Everybody came from a special terrain, so the situation was not the same in all the areas. It was not identical. It wasn't even close to being the same. Some people expressed large degree of concern, some did not, they were not as concerned. So that was where the difference lay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any significant differences as to what various deputies, SDS deputies, in the Serb Assembly suggested should be done?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Some were more radical, some were less radical. But the situation on the ground was already very complicated and probably difficult. I can tell you what I know about Tuzla. Already at that time after the recognition of Bosnia on the part of the international community, there was the situation when people were removed from all the bodies -- all the Serbs were removed from all the bodies in the municipality of Tuzla. And that is something that tells you a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we just leave Tuzla for the moment, please, Mr. Micic. Just staying with the Bosnian Serb Assembly, when you said "some were more radical, some were less radical," can you be specific as to what the more radical elements were saying that was different from the less radical?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The more radical people wanted for -- wanted arms to be distributed, to start armed conflicts, to seek help from outside. The JNA was still there, but they were not doing anything. They thought that they were in the garrison and they were not doing anything. Those were the requests by the radicals, for the arms to be distributed. The others, the less radical ones, were against that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said "to seek help from outside," did you understand what that meant?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't think it was important where it came from, as long as it was some sort of aid. I thought that anybody should be brought in, but those ideas just did not fall on fertile ground.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who did you understand who could be brought in from outside?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I remember that Mrs. Biljana Plavsic mentioned Arkan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mrs. Plavsic -- she -- in what way did she mention Arkan?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: As a man who could help Serbs. That's the way she was thinking. I mean in military terms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was she specific about how Arkan could help Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No, she was not specific. But I remember that she kept on repeating that any kind of help from anywhere in the world, America, Australia, from volunteers, that all those were welcome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Mrs. Plavsic supported in these views by other members of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Not many.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember, so as to be able to identify them, anybody who did clearly support Mrs. Plavsic in those views?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I believe that those are minutes from those Assembly sessions. I'm sure that they can be located.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking you specifically about your recollection, Mr. Micic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It's hard for me to say, some more, some less. You know, it's very difficult to go back in time. It was some 14, 15 years ago, or 13 years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able, from your recollection, to identify members of the Assembly who clearly did not support Mrs. Plavsic in those views?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. That position was mostly supported by the people who were already members of the Territorial Defence, who had already established some paramilitary formations in their respective municipalities who already had some armed groups of people. They supported or had the others condemn her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was asking if you could identify members of the Assembly who did not support Mrs. Plavsic in those views. If you are able to do so, please would you do so.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: For example, MPs from Bijeljina did not support her in her views. I believe that even MPs from Sarajevo did not support her. Mostly MPs from Eastern Bosnia did not support her.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any members of the Assembly who were in the army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: You mean as active-service members of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any -- was there anybody present in the Assemblies since, speaking was an active-service member of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Throughout all this time while the JNA was in Bosnia, I don't remember that any members of the JNA were there. When the Army of Republika Srpska was established, then yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At that point when the Army of Serb Republic or Republika Srpska was established, who then was present at Assembly sessions who was a serving member of that army?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Very often General Mladic, General Gvero as well, sometimes General Talic, General Tolimir. It all depended on the area where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- do you recall General Mladic's -- an expression of views by General Mladic as to how the Bosnian Serbs should proceed from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: He presented plans, the assessments of the situation, and he called for the state of war to be declared. He often did that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember anybody who was specifically opposed to General Mladic's view on that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Opposed to the declaration of a state of war and general mobilisation, the removal of all the civilian bodies of a power was Mr. Krajisnik and also Mr. Karadzic. They were categorically against those things, both of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any differences in Mr. Krajisnik's conduct of the Presidency of the Serb Assembly as compared to the way in which he had conducted the Presidency of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: There was no difference. He acted in accordance with the book of rules and the constitution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I just seek a clarification on the subject which you seem to have left but I'd like to better understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In one of your previous answers you told us that the radicals also requested the arms to be distributed. What exactly do you mean,"arms to be distributed," by whom? To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't understand me. I did not mean the radicals as a political party. I meant those members of the Assembly who had a more radical position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes -- no, I think I fully understood you in that respect. When I was talking about radicals, I was not talking about a political party, but I was talking about people who were more on the radical side than others. So you said they requested for the arms to be distributed. By whom? To whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until the moment the JNA left Bosnia and Herzegovina, the depots of arms of the Territorial Defence were under the control of the army in the barracks. They asked for those weapons. And I believe that the owner of those weapons were the municipalities or the Territorial Defence. They wanted the army to give them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you say: "They were under the control of the army in the barracks. They asked for those weapons, and I believe that the owner of those weapons were the municipalities." So they insisted on giving the arms to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the Territorial Defence that was in that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Irrespective of what kind of municipality that was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those who came from those municipalities who had established that there, they were the ones who asked for that. But it was common practice in the entire territory. Everybody wanted arms, in the places where the Muslims were a majority, where the Croats were a majority, where the Serbs were a majority. There was no difference there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But do I have to -- then to understand that in the Serb Assembly, those who were more radical requested arms to be given to municipalities where there was a Muslim majority so that the weapons would become available for Muslims? Is that what I have to understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Or was it that they wanted the arms under the control of the JNA to be given to the municipality where there was a Serb majority? Is that how I have to understand it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everybody asked for their respective municipalities, but that was a common practice in all and every municipalities, irrespective of which municipality it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did understand you. But I'm talking about what radicals proposed in the Bosnian Serb Assembly. So -- and you said -- did I now understand you well that in this Bosnian Serb Assembly they were asking for the weapons to be given to the municipality with a Serbian majority or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The request was not to be applied to the entire territory of Bosnia where there was a Serb majority. There were specific requests coming from specific municipalities for a specific problem. If somebody came from Sarajevo, they made requests in respect of Sarajevo. If somebody came from Brcko, they requested something in respect of Brcko. They were not interested in any other municipality in Bosnia, and this is what I call more radical people, with more radical requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you used the word "distribution." To whom would they have to be distributed? I mean handing over the control of certain depots is not yet distribution. To whom should these weapons be distributed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would have been taking out weapons from under the control of the army, the weapons that were in their safe-keeping. And it was to be done by the Territorial Defence of that particular municipality, and the MP coming from such a municipality would raise that issue as a specific problem of that municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I still have not fully comprehended what you meant by "distribution" then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't mean that somebody would distribute weapons. I don't know how the weapons would have been distributed. In any case, their intention was to take the weapons from the garrison and the weapons that were the ownership of the Territorial Defence, and that was being safeguarded by the army. They wanted that weapon -- those weapons to be taken from the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Judge Hanoteau has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Stewart asked you this. [In English] "Did you have at that time in March 1992 any significant different view from Dr. Karadzic on any of the current political issues?" [Interpretation] And you answered: [In English] "The only thing I wanted was to avoid any kind of conflict." [Interpretation] Does this mean that Dr. Karadzic did not share your wish?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The situation on the ground was such that we received constant information about the arming of people and the entering of weapons into Bosnia and Herzegovina from Croatia. We knew that the Patriotic League was being armed under different names. There were constant discussions as to what should be done once they are fully armed, and somebody said: We will defend ourselves. And I thought that we have had to talk, and that was the difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, did you at any time in the second half of 1991 or the first three months of 1992 attend any political meetings in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the answer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps you just repeat the answer into the microphone, Mr. Micic, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On one occasion or more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, I believe I was there maybe three times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The first time the meeting was held once we had walked out of the Assembly; the second time was the constituent Assembly of the Serbian people; and the third meeting was a working meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's take them one by one in that order then. The -- you say: "The first time the meeting was held once we had walked out of the Assembly." So you're meaning immediately after or very shortly after the 14th, 15th of October, 1991, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No, not immediately. I believe that this meeting was held in the blue room in the building of the BH Assembly. That was the hall normally used by the Council of Citizens.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Seeking to clarify. Let's just focus on your answer. You said the first time that there was such a meeting at the Holiday Inn was once -- you said "we had walked out of the Assembly." Let's just be clear. When you say "walked out of the Assembly" --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes. Immediately after we walked out of the Assembly, but I did not consider that to be a very important meeting. We focussed more on the comments as to what they would do there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to be clear. First of all, you say -- when you say "immediately after we walked out of the Assembly," by talking of walking out of the Assembly, do you mean the occasion on the 14th, 15th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll move on to the second time then. You said the second time there was a meeting at the Holiday Inn that you remember attending was the constituent Assembly of the Serbian people. Now, first of all, are you saying that an Assembly meeting itself was held in the Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: It's very hard for me to say whether it was in the Holiday Inn or in the blue room. It was one of the two in any case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you were referring to an actual Assembly meeting, are you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you said the third meeting was a working meeting. Now, before I ask you about the nature of that meeting, are you able to say when that third meeting took place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would be able to give any helpful indication as to the date, if not exact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I believe it was in spring 1992. Probably in April. Or maybe March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you say it was a working meeting, meaning what? A working meeting as opposed to what other sort of meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: A special, as a special occasion. There are special-occasion meetings in celebration of something or a working meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was a working meeting of what or whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Of the Assembly of the Serbian People.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Held in a Holiday Inn?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you -- in 1991 or 1992, did you ever attend any meeting in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo of a wider nature, including not only members of the Assembly but others?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nature of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the agenda. There were a lot of people at that meeting. There were a lot of guests as well. There were also members of the Main Board of the SDS who were present there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remember what the purpose of the meeting was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I can't remember what the agenda was, but I believe that it was dedicated to the organisation of work of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you remember who presided over that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The sessions were always presided over by Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sessions of what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik ever preside over any other sorts of meetings, apart from sessions of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were also the Deputies' Club meetings of the SDS party deputies, which he did not preside over. But there were probably other meetings that I don't know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever attend Deputies' Club meetings of the SDS party deputies?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think that I did once or maybe twice, but very briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who presided?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Vojislav Maksimovic, Professor Maksimovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of a document known as Variants A and B or some such similar name?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever been to a large political meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo where any documentation was distributed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Each Assembly session -- at each Assembly session, documents were distributed, so I don't remember anything in particular. But every time the Assembly discussed something, then the relevant documents were distributed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Tuzla --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before you continue -- The last question put to you was: "Have you ever been to a large political meeting at the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo where any documentation was distributed?" And then your answer was: "Each Assembly session -- at each Assembly session, documents were distributed." Were now Assembly sessions usually held in the Holiday Inn, and do you call a large political meeting, is that an Assembly session or ... I'm just trying to understand your answer in relation to the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not possible at the time to have the deputies receive the regular or proper Assembly documents. It was -- there wasn't enough time so -- to have them given out in advance. So usually what happened was that this material was given to the deputies once they came to the meeting. That's what I meant, these Assembly materials. As far as attendances at the Assembly sessions, there were always many people present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but I did put two specific questions to you. First: Were Assembly sessions usually held in the Holiday Inn? That's the first one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was about a large political meeting at the Holiday Inn. Was there ever an Assembly session held in the Holiday Inn in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I said that it was once or twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Once or twice. And you say --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- there were many others as well. If a question is about a large political meeting, you would include in that formulation an Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it cannot be understood in that way. An Assembly meeting is an Assembly meeting, but there was no perfect discipline at the Assembly only to have sessions by deputies of the Assembly. Very often there were others present: Certain members of the Main Board who were there from the SDS or a president of the municipality, somebody from the army, somebody from the clergy. So every time somebody would be present. So this is what I would call a meeting. But however, the Assembly sessions were also held at the same time. The Assembly sessions were conducted regardless of the presence of these other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It still confuses me a bit because the question was about a large political meeting, and your answer was about Assembly sessions. Now, when I ask you whether an Assembly session would be something within the scope of what you understand to be a large political meeting, you said: "No, it cannot be understood in that way." So you leave me with quite some confusion in this respect. If you can clarify it, please do so; otherwise, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I can. No problem. I said that the Assembly sessions were usually attended by certain guests, whether they were from the ranks of the Main Board of the SDS or if they were from the area where the Assembly session was being held. There was always somebody from the Orthodox church clergy present also. There were also people who were there. I mean, I don't know all the people who would come inside. They were sitting there. But as far as I was concerned, it wasn't an organised political meeting of the type THAT you are thinking of. It was an Assembly where anybody, practically, could walk in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't thinking about anything. It was part of the question put to you by Mr. Stewart. But let's proceed, Mr. Stewart, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic, you told Their Honours earlier today that after the 1990 elections, November 1990, it was your party and the League of Communists who were in control of Tuzla. That was what you've already said. Did that change subsequently?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Yes, it did change, quite radically as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did that change occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: The changes occurred after the declaration on the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted, and in particular after the international community's recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And -- well, we -- do you remember when that was, the international community's recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I think that it was in late March or early April 1992, but I'm not sure. The declaration on an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina was voted on the 14th and 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- so you told Their Honours that the changes occurred particularly after the international community's recognition of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but also you said "after the declaration on the independence." When did -- let's start with when did significant changes first occur in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Right after the declaration on an independent autonomous Bosnia and Herzegovina was voted on. There was certain shifts in the thinking of people who were in power at the time. At that point, the Municipal Assembly of Tuzla also had its own National Defence Councils, and there were only Muslims in these councils. And it was my fault, perhaps, that this happened like that. There wasn't a single Croat in them even. Then the chief of the Tuzla region internal affairs department was replaced. Also some judges of the municipal and the higher court in Tuzla were also replaced. And then it went on like in a chain reaction to encompass the professors at schools, at universities, and then also in the town's clinics, because Tuzla was a university town. Even the dean of the university, who was with us at the SRS, very quickly moved to the SDA and became a prominent member of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've said that the -- it went on like in a chain reaction to encompass the professors at schools, at universities, and then you referred to the university. What happened and when in relation to the university?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: These professors were replaced. There was also a boycott of certain professors. The students conducted this boycott. A known case or an example of that was that in the hospitals if there was a Serb who was a prominent professor, and Bozidar Radovic was one of these people. He was a very reputable world medical expert. He also had some uncomfortable situations. For example, if he went in to see a woman patient, she said: I don't want to be examined by a Vlah, a Serb. That was the term used. It was an attack or an assault on everything that was Serb, even though this professor, Radovic, was somebody who enjoyed a very high reputation in Tuzla before that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when did this occur?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: This began in late 1991 and early 1992. The parties -- so that you understand. The Tuzla municipality was actually in the hands, in the talons of the region, the regional board of Tuzla, and the Tuzla regional board was under the control of the SDA. So according to the party affiliation, the professors, the judges, were replaced because this was taken to be one of the rights of the party. And that's when many of them left, not only the SUP, not only did the Serbs leave, but many Muslims also left, those who did not accept membership of the SDA. They, too, were driven away from their posts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've referred to Serbs leaving. Can you indicate to Their Honours what scale of Serbs leaving do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Well, you cannot talk about a mass exodus, such as the one from the territory of Croatia where there was an armed conflict. It was just a question of a slow tide. Every day people were leaving Tuzla. They were going in all directions, and I assert that out of 20.000 Serbs and about 20.000 Yugoslavs, on the 15th of May when there was a settling of accounts with the Yugoslav People's Army, there weren't more than 4.000, both Serbs and Yugoslavs, left in Tuzla at that time. Now I don't think that there are any of them left in Tuzla now. They just simply left town and I was among them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just clarify. You say "there weren't more than 4.000, both Serbs and Yugoslavs, left in Tuzla at that time." Do you mean 4.000 Serbs and 4.000 Yugoslavs? Or 4.000 altogether, embracing both Serbs and Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: I cannot really tell you the exact number for the Yugoslavs, but the Yugoslavs included a smaller number of also Muslims and Croats. After Yugoslavia was abolished, this term "Yugoslav" also disappeared. So they returned to their national or ethnic core. In Tuzla, after the 15th of May, not more than 4.000 Yugoslavs and Serbs remained living in Tuzla. This is after the 15th of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We haven't quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was going to say, Your Honour, we haven't quite cleared up the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Micic. I'm just seeking clarification of your answer. When you talk about 4.000 Yugoslav and Serbs, do you mean -- you said you can't be precise. But are you talking about 4.000 Yugoslavs and 4.000 Serbs, or are you talking about 4.000 altogether?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: A total of 4.000 people of Serb ethnicity that remained in Tuzla, regardless of whether they were from the ranks of those 20.000 who had declared themselves as Serbs or from among those who had declared themselves as Yugoslavs. Because after the 15th of May, Tuzla became a closed environment. The town was encircled. It was not possible to leave after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it still doesn't seem to answer your question directly. May I give it another effort. The 4.000 remaining, would that -- I do understand there were Serbs remaining. The number of 4.000, did that also include those who had declared themselves Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So I take it, then, that we have a single number of 4.000. I would seek some clarification of one of your previous answers as well. You said that professors were replaced. And then you continued in your answer describing how, for example, Professor Radovic felt quite uncomfortable in those circumstances, and you were talking about boycotts by students and patients not wishing to be examined by a professor. Replacing - but please disagree with me if you have a different understanding of that word - is to put someone in the place previously occupied by another. It is ambiguous to the extent that you either take one person from a position and put another there or that someone feels very uncomfortable in the position, leaves, and that you fill in the vacancy which you have not explicitly created yourself, although it may have been under the circumstances that one could expect someone to leave. Now, when you are talking about replacement, are you talking about some people leaving in the circumstances you described which are characterised by being very unpleasant for the person and then the vacancy re-filled, or were professors or the others you mentioned, were they just fired and then replaced by someone else? Perhaps you could start with the example of Professor Radovic. Was he fired or did he leave under the circumstances that you described and was then replaced by someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start from the regional SUP. As soon as the regional SUP chief was replaced, automatically all the others in the SUP were replaced who were not loyal to the SDA, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Muslims, or Croats. As far as Professor Radovic is concerned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there because you do not answer my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I will. I will tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The regional SUP chief, was he fired and then replaced by someone else or did he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's a clear answer. Those others you said who are automatically replaced because they were not loyal to the SDA, were they fired and then replaced or did they leave and then --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They were fired. Okay. Now we come to Professor Radovic. Same question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor Radovic was not dismissed. He was the chief of the clinic, and he was replaced as the head of the clinic, and he continued to work as a regular surgeon. As far as the university is concerned, simply the university council or board voted someone else to replace these people from their posts. They didn't dismiss them, but they just replaced them. So there were also cases where these people who had been replaced felt in danger, so they would leave Tuzla for a day or two until things settled down a bit, but then as soon as they were away from Tuzla for two or three days, then they would be dismissed from their job. So that's basically the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart. Oh, just Hanoteau whispers in my ear that he has a question as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely regarding that exodus of Serbs and Yugoslavs, how do you explain it? Did it occur after this institutional violence or were there any other violences? And by institutional violences, I mean this obligation to leave, to change their employment, or was this something else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot just look at one element as a key element in that period. There were checkpoints set up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: An element?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Checkpoints were set up, and these checkpoints were set up in the town itself. So if you wanted to defend Tuzla, then the checkpoints should have been set up on the outskirts of the Tuzla municipality. But they were placed in the neighbourhoods where the Muslims were a majority and they were facing the neighbourhoods where the Serbs were the majority population. There was constant harassment also. At the time, I enjoyed immunity. And from my apartment to my place of work, they were about three kilometres apart, and I would have to pass through four checkpoints. If I came back within a very short period of time, I would still have to go back through all of those checkpoints. If I returned home, I would have to go through the checkpoint that was located in my building. So this is what the atmosphere was like, and people began to feel afraid. So one by one they simply fled, they left, and then also on top of that when you had dismissals from their posts. All the posts that were of a regional significance were automatically purged of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Those checkpoints were manned by whom exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were manned by the Patriotic League. It -- they were not wearing the sign or the insignia of the lily, but they were using the Tuzla coat of arms. And by using that Tuzla coat of arms, they were trying to conceal their real name. And they were part of the broader forces of the Tuzla MUP. And I mentioned him earlier, Mehmed Bajric, was the one who led that particular group. I mentioned that he went to the SDA in order to remain at this post. Later he even became the president of the SDA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, Witness, how can you tell with certainty that these people were people from the Patriotic League if they wore different uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were the same uniforms; it was just a question of different insignia. Those same people from that same league attacked the column of soldiers that was leaving Tuzla on the 15th of May, and they killed approximately 200 people. According to some, it was 80 people; and according to others, it was 200; according to information of the medical centre, it was 204; however, the exact number was never established. But these are the same people. Even today that day is celebrated as the day of independence. Independence from what? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, we interrupted the flow of evidence. There are three minutes left. If you can deal with any subject in three minutes, fine; if not, then perhaps it's better to stop for the day and adjourn.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there's a couple of small points which would be useful just to sweep up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The name of the regional police chief that you said was replaced was what?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: Budimir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the checkpoints about which His Honour Judge Hanoteau has just been asking you, when did they first appear?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO MICIC
utterances.text: They appeared right at the start, I think already in November 1991, with the idea of forming an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina and passing a vote on that through the Bosnia and Herzegovina Assembly and along with some ideas that the local SDS had. And they had some aspirations in relation to Tuzla. So that's where these disputes arose, but I really don't know what the substance or the essence of the disputes actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, those were the couple of points I wanted to clear up now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Mr. Micic, we'll finish for the day. I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony you have given today and you're still about to give in the days to come. We'd like to see you back tomorrow in this same courtroom at a -- in Courtroom I at a quarter past 2.00. Madam Usher, could you please escort Mr. Micic out of the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, it has turned out to be now and then useful to inquire into the estimate given by the Defence on how much time they would need for the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For this witness I think it was scheduled for six hours. Are you going to need those six hours? We had a short day today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I probably would need -- well, yes, or near enough, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that certainly assists us in knowing what's -- so that would take approximately the whole of tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to do my best overnight, as I think we always do on both sides, to see what I can pare down in the light of today. But I can't be overly optimistic at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. It's your time, it's your witness. So then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I believe, Your Honour, I've had -- we started just after 3.00 today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You've spent only two hours and 15 minutes until now. So it's not any kind of criticism, but just for us to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I certainly don't want to be too pessimistic. Your Honour said that take approximately the whole of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. One day in court gives an effective four hours of examination-in-chief. And if you have estimated this witness for six hours, then after two and a quarter, there remains three and three-quarters to go, and that's close to four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I was taking a positive view, Your Honour. I wouldn't be taking the whole of tomorrow. I was trying to be encouraging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, it's fine. As I started these words that it's -- that it has turned now and then out to be useful to inquire into the estimate given.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart's just trying to show he's sort of the glass-is-half-full kind of guy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If there's 15 minutes left in the session, he hasn't used he whole thing, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I am that kind of guy, Your Honour, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not start. I always wish there to be glasses with one-quarter on the top empty and one-quarter on the bottom, but unfortunately they do not exist. So, therefore, the half-full or the half-empty is -- is our fate. So we will adjourn until tomorrow, Courtroom I, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
